IN
THE
spring of
1925,
when
the
experimental
work
on
the high-pres-
sure
synthesis
of methanol
from carbon monoxide and
hydrogen
was
initiated in
this laboratory, considerable
publicity had already
been
given to the hew methanol
synthesis, although actual
data
on operation of the
process
were
meager.
A
German patent of
19132
covered the process of syn-
thesizing oxygenated organic
compounds from carbon
monoxide and hydrogen in a
broad and general way, while
more
specific information was
available in a patent and
a
paper by Patart.3 An article by Audibert also appeared at that
time.4
From these sources it was apparent that methanol
could be produced by passing a mixture of carbon monoxide
and hydrogen over
a heated metallic oxide catalyst at high
pressure.

a number of patents claim the

even methanol.7
From a consideration of the
volumes entering in the reac-
tions it is apparent that the
formation of methanol goes
with the largest volume de-
crease—viz., from three to one
and
hence would
be most
favored by increased pressure.
The parallelism between the methanol reaction and the
reaction for synthesis of ammonia is striking in this respect.
Calculations of the methanol equilibrium
are
bound to
be more
or
less inaccurate owing to the lack of adequate
data on the specific heat and the equation of state of the
alcohol.
The fact that the synthesis is carried out at tem-
peratures of 300° C. and up—that is, in the neighborhood of
and above the critical temperature of methanol (240° C.)—
further reduces the quantitative significance of equilibrium
calculations.
In
a
. qualitative way,

varies with temperature.

A study has been made of some
of the factors govern-
ing the synthesis of methanol
from carbon monoxide
and hydrogen under high pressure and in the presence
of
a catalyst.
The literature
on
methanol
catalysts
is discussed in the light of experimental data, and the
methanol equilibrium as calculated from thermal data
is compared with results obtained with
a catalyst com-
posed of the oxides of copper, zinc, and aluminum.
The methanol
formed by the reaction
has a purity
of between 99 and 100 per cent provided that the vari-
ables temperature, pressure, and rate of flow are chosen
within
the limits
most desirable from the point of view
of maximum
yield.
Under these same
conditions only
a small
amount
of carbon monoxide is lost in wasteful
side reactions, leading
to
the
formation
of carbon
dioxide, methane, and water.
Studies made with
sev-
eral chambers
in
series have demonstrated that
the
catalyst contained in the first
chamber protects the
catalyst in successive chambers against poisoning.

It
is interesting to note that the equilibrium constant
of the reaction changes with temperature in such a manner
that at atmospheric pressure and room temperature methanol
would be perfectly stable, while at 300° C. equilibrium
would be attained with less than 2 per cent methanol, starting
with
a mixture of carbon monoxide and hydrogen in the
theoretical ratio
of
1:2.
Even with
the
best
catalysts
it has apparently been impossible to suppress the reaction
temperature much below 300° C., corresponding practically
to no methanol at atmospheric pressure.
This clearly shows
why past attempts to synthesize methanol from the gases
in question at atmospheric pressure were
bound to meet
with failure.
On the other hand, the calculations indicate
that at a pressure of 1000 pounds per square inch,
or

atmospheres, the equilibrium would still be favorable to
practically 100 per cent methanol at 300° C.
Even with
selective catalysts it becomes desirable, however, to employ
considerably higher pressure in order to favor methanol
formation at the expense of the two methane reactions.
Furthermore, it is to be expected that the rate of reaction
increases with pressure owing to the higher concentrations.
Figures 1 and 2 give the calculated percentages of carbon
monoxide converted to methanol at equilibrium for any com-
bination of temperature
and
pressure.
The calculations
are for a gas mixture containing 26 per cent carbon monoxide
and 70 per cent hydrogen in order to permit direct comparison
with the experimental results reported later in this paper.
Types of Catalysts Used in
Synthesis of Methanol
In addition to the papers and patents cited above, there
has appeared during the last two years a great deal of in-
formation relative to the types of catalysts suitable for
methanol formation.10
The most important group of catalysts
consists of combinations of non-reducible metallic oxides in
which it is generally essential to have the most basic com-
ponent
present in
preponderating
quantities.11
While
a
number of the first patents claimed the necessity of complete
exclusion of iron from the reaction zone, it is now
generally
agreed that iron may be present, presumably in a non-active
form.12

The term “non-reducible,” when referring to the oxides
used as catalysts, becomes rather indefinite.
A compound
like zinc oxide, for example, which normally is not reduced
by carbon monoxide
or
hydrogen at the temperatures in
question (300° to 400° C.) shows all indications of being at
least partially reduced, when intimately mixed with copper
oxide.13
It
has
even
been
stated14 that metallic oxides
which, when alone, are reduced to the corresponding metals
do not completely part with their oxygen when mixed with
more basic oxides.
Patart3 claims to have based his catalyst search in con-
nection with the methanol synthesis,
on
the observations
by Sabatier and Maihle16 and Jahn16 on the reverse reaction—
i. e., the catalytic decomposition of methanol at elevated
temperatures.
After having tried a number of the individual
catalysts studied by these investigators, Patart, however,
ultimately came to the conclusion that mixed catalysts were
required for best results, although the data disclosed in his
first paper would indicate that zinc oxide alone is a good
catalyst.
Similar observations on
zinc oxide
are
reported
by Fischer,17 but the present writers have not had much
success
with
catalysts
consisting
of
a
single
oxide.
In
general, it has been found advantageous to use mixtures of
two or more
metallic oxides of which one, at least, is non-
reducible with reference to carbon monoxide and hydrogen
under atmospheric pressure at the temperature in question.
Owing to the exothermic character of the methanol re-
action, 26,150 calories per mol of gaseous methanol formed
at 327° C., it
was found beneficial to support the catalyst
on
a good heat conductor in order to prevent local over-
heating of the contact material.
Granulated metallic copper
proved satisfactory for this purpose.
While a large number of catalysts have been studied, the
data reported below were
all obtained with a mixture origi-
nally consisting of 36 per cent zinc oxide, 44 per cent copper
oxide, and 20 per cent aluminum oxide supported on metallic
copper, the ratio of active catalyst to copper support being
1:3.
This catalyst is of medium activity.

The hydroxides
of the metals in question are
precipitated by ammonium
hydroxide from an aqueous solution of the nitrates at 85° C.,
the purest grade of chemicals being used throughout.
Upon
careful washing, the hydroxides are obtained as
a gel into
which the supporting copper is mixed prior to drying at
110° C.
A granular, rugged catalyst may thus be obtained.
After having been placed in the reactor, the catalyst is
brought up to a temperature of 180° to 200° C. and subjected
to the action of the carbon monoxide-hydrogen mixture
under reduced pressure, say 100 to 400 pounds per square
inch (6.8 to 26.1 atmospheres), for 2 to 4 hours.
During
this
process the
copper
oxide
is presumably reduced to
metallic
copper,
while
the hydrated
aluminum
oxide
is
dehydrated
partly,
but
probably
not
completely.
Re-
duction to lower stages of oxidation of the zinc and aluminum
may also take place, since this has been shown to be the case
for zinc oxide mixed with copper oxide, as mentioned above.
Apparatus
A diagrammatic layout of the apparatus used for the
synthesis of methanol is shown in Figure 3.
The essential
features are (1) mixing of the carbon monoxide and hydrogen
in desired proportions, (2) compression of the gas mixture,
(3) oil filtration, (4) further purification of gases if desired,
(5) storage of compressed gas to provide for intermittent
compression, (6) regulation of pressure of outflowing gas by
means
of proper reducing valves,
(7) reaction of carbon
monoxide and hydrogen in electrically heated chrome vana-
dium steel reactors, (8) condensation under pressure of the
liquid product in water-cooled condensers,
(9) separation
of liquid from gas, followed
by (10) discharge of liquid
and gas through
separate
valves and (11) determina-
tion of liquid yield and of
exit gas flow.
Valves
are
installed for withdrawal of
gas samples for analysis and
special holders
are
con-
nected with the exit gas lines
to permit collection of com-
posite
samples.
The dia-
gram also shows alternative
connections for operation of
two
or
three chambers in
series.
High-pressure flow-
meters may be inserted at
the entrance to the reactors,
although the entering gas
flow can readily be followed
from the exit rate when cor-
rection
is made for the
products formed
per unit
time.
The reaction chambers
are constructed of chrome-
vanadium steel with bolted-
on heads.
They are'copper-
lined and provided with
thermocouple wells permit-
ting measurement
of the
temperature of the
gas in
the reaction zone
or at any
other point throughout the
reactor.
The catalyst

Effect of Different
Variables
on
Operation of Methanol
Process
With a mixture of carbon monoxide and hydrogen flowing
through the reactor at pressures from about 1000 pounds per
square inch (68 atmospheres) and up, methanol begins to
form as soon
as the temperature of the catalyst has reached
about 300° C.
The minimum reaction temperature varies
with the catalyst and decreases somewhat with increasing
pressure, but rarely goes below 280° C.
While the thermodynamic calculations presented graphi-
cally in Figures
1 and 2 predict the temperature and pres-
sure
ranges within which the process may be operated most
successfully, they fail to take into account two
essential
variables:
(1) rate of reaction,
or
space-time yield, and
the effect of temperature on it; and (2) change in activity
of the catalyst with time and temperature,
as well
as its
susceptibility to poisoning.
Hence it
becomes
necessary
to study the effect of these different factors by actual ex-
periments.
Figure 4 gives the rate of methanol formation as a function
of the rate of entering gas flow under a constant pressure of
3000 pounds per square inch (204 atmospheres).
It appears
that the yield of methanol is a linear function of the rate
of gas flow.
No attempt will be made to explain this result
at present, since the effect of rate of diffusion and other
factors involved are not known.
From Figure 4 it will also be noticed that the methanol yield
decreases with increasing
temperature.
No data are
given on this plot for 300°
C., because it was impossi-
ble to get a representative
curve
from the observations
made at that temperature
in this series of experiments.
The irregular results at 300
°
C. are
not surprising when
it is considered that this is,
practically speaking, the
temperature at which the
reaction starts, and it is well
known that results are hard
to reproduce at the point
where a catalyst commences
to become active, especially
when the reaction in ques-
tion is exothermic.
While
the quantity of
methanol formed per unit
time increases with the rate
of gas flow, the percentage
conversion of carbon mon-
oxide decreases owing to the
shorter time of contact be-
tween the reacting gas and
the
catalyst.
Percentage
conversion
vs. rate of flow
is plotted in Figure 5 for
various temperatures at
3000 pounds pressure
(204
atmospheres).
The
curve
for 300° C. is somewhat un-
certain
on account of the
wide variations in the ob-

Figure 6 shows this graphically for another series of experi-

Again the conversion

Figure 7 shows the percentage conversion of carbon mon-
oxide to methanol as a function of temperature at 3000 pounds
pressure (204 atmospheres) and an entering gas flow of 100
liters per hour.
The upper curve
represents the theoretical
conversion at equilibrium as calculated from thermal data.
The plot does not permit any conclusions as to the validity
of the thermodynamic calculations, since these calculations
are based on equilibrium conditions, while the experimental
results are obtained at a rate of flow at which we know for a
certainty that equilibrium is not attained.
The interesting
point about these curves
is that they bring out the decrease
in the activity of the catalyst with increasing temperature.
Even though the calculated curve
may not be exactly correct
owing to the uncertainty attached to the calculations, its
course
is characteristic of this type of reactions.
Hence,
the experimental curve
should have displayed a somewhat
similar slope had the activity of the catalyst stayed constant.
This particular way of plotting the results, therefore, permits
a study of the change in activity with rising temperature.

by the fact that a catalyst, once

Character
of Methanol
Formed
The alcohol produced by reaction of carbon monoxide and
hydrogen at, say, 3000 pounds pressure (204 atmospheres)
and at not too high a temperature is very pure, as evidenced
by
a
specific gravity corresponding to
99-100 per cent
methanol.
The odor is that of pure methanol, and combustion
analysis gives
a ratio of carbon to hydrogen and oxygen
corresponding to the formula CHsOH.

side reactions do not occur

The ratio of methane

In this par-

the percentage carbon monoxide going to side

is higher than usual.

In order to study the length of catalyst life,
a series of
experiments
was
run
in which
no
attempt
was
made to
purify the gas mixture, consisting of electrolytic hydrogen
and of carbon monoxide from the decomposition of formic
acid with sulfuric acid.
The catalyst was
the one already
mentioned, prepared from the oxides of copper, zinc, and
aluminum
and
supported
on
granulated
copper.

Conclusions
Methanol of high purity may readily be prepared by
passing a mixture of carbon monoxide and hydrogen, pref-
erably at a pressure of several hundred atmospheres and at
temperatures between 300° and 350° C.,
over
a catalyst
composed of metallic oxides.
Working with
a catalyst of
medium activity prepared from the oxides of copper, zinc,
and aluminum, it
is possible to reach nearly theoretical
conversion depending upon the pressure, temperature, and
rate of gas flow employed.
Carbon dioxide, water, and
methane may form, but the amount of carbon monoxide
consumed in these side reactions is small under the conditions
most favorable to methanol formation.
The catalyst in
question, consisting of the oxides of copper, zinc, and alu-
minum supported on metallic copper, appears to be most
active at lower temperature and suffers
a permanent de-
crease
in activity when exposed to higher temperatures.
Also the catalyst is sensitive to poisons.
By connecting
several chambers in series, however, it is possible to dispose
of the catalyst poison in the first chamber, thus protecting
the contact material contained in subsequent reactors.
